BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, game AI perception and pathfinding. Thirty-three terms for game characters that act on their own from what a guard can see and hear to how it steers and finds a route. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent what to build.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often say a guard sees the player whenever it is in range. Range is only the first test. The player must also be inside the guard's cone on a straight line no wall blocks. Game AI is full of lookalike pairs like that. This film goes through the terms group by group each one shown so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Outside source, the term comes from a source outside the course text. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea. With no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map 33 terms of game AI in four groups in the order an agent works. It senses then steers then follows a route. The first group is perceiving. Agent Sense Decide Act Site Range Field of Yukon Line of Sight Hearing Radius and Last Known Position.

B0102.heard: The second group is steering. Steering itself, velocity and max speed, seek, flee, arrive, pursue and wander. These terms say how an agent moves toward things or away from them, a little on every tick.

B0103.heard: The third group is groups and crowds, separation, alignment, cohesion, emergent behavior and local avoidance. These terms say how many agents move together without bumping into each other or scattering.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Maps and Search. Graph, Grid, Navigation Mesh, Waypoint, Breadth first search, Dykstra, A-Star, F, G, and H, heuristics, the open and closed set, Path Smoothing and Navigation Agent 2D. These terms say how an agent finds a route through a level.

B0201.heard: A single guard in an empty room in a simulated run, an agent is a game character that senses the world and acts on its own with no player pressing its buttons. This guard decides for itself to walk between two waypoints at 100 pixels per second. For example, the guard the course adds to a walker project is an agent. It patrols a loop of waypoints and it switches to a chase when it spots the player.

B0202.heard: Now a player's square walks toward the guard. Sense, decide, act as the loop an agent runs once per tick. It senses, hear the distance to the player. It decides, hear closer than 200 pixels means chase. It acts by setting its velocity. The three boxes light up in turn. For example, a turret in your level senses each tick, whether the player is in reach, decides to fire or wait, and acts by spawning a bullet.

B0203.heard: A noise goes off at the red dot. The hearing radius or noise radius is how far a noise carries to an agent. It counts distance only and ignores which way the agent faces. The ring is 250 pixels, so two of the three guards hear it, and the one at 333 pixels does not. For example, a player knocks over a crate, and every guard within its noise radius turns toward the sound, even guards looking the other way.

B0204.heard: The player slips behind a wall. Last known position is where the target was last seen, kept in the agent's memory. The Red Cross marks it. The guard walks to that spot, which takes three seconds here, searches, and then goes back where it started. For example, the Walker Guard search state takes it to the last known player position, where it waits, and then it returns to patrol.

B0301.heard: Two guards, G1 and G2, and 12 dots to spot. Sight range is how far an NPC a non-player character can see. It is a distance and nothing else. Every dot inside a guard circle of 340 pixels counts, even one behind a wall. Here each guard counts four and six dots are seen by either. For example, a sentry tower that wakes up whenever the player comes within a set distance, walls or no walls. Use is only a sight range.

B0302.heard: Now each guard has a cone. The field of view cone is the angle across which an agent can see, centred on the way it faces. A dot must be in range and also inside the 70 degree cone. As the cones sweep, the counts rise and fall. For example, a guard in a stealth level who faces the door cannot see the player creeping up from behind, however near the player gets.

B0303.heard: A wall now stands in the middle. Line of sight means a straight line from the agent to the target that nothing blocks. Dots in the wall's shadow drop out. With all three tests each guard sees two and three dots are seen by either. Site range is only a distance and line of sight also needs that clear line. For example, the walker guard casts a ray toward the player and a player hidden behind the obstacle does not make it chase.

B0401.heard: An agent turns toward a red target in a simulated run. Velocity is speed with a direction, and max speed caps its size, here 160 pixels per second. Steering is the family of behaviors that change that velocity a little each tick, the desired velocity minus the current one. For example, the Walker player's run speed is capped at 162, and a bat enemy that curves toward the player instead of snapping around is steering.

B0402.heard: Seek means steer toward a target. It aims straight at the target at full speed on every tick and never slows. So it reaches the target at 160 pixels per second over shoots and circles back and the speed line below swings up and down. For example, a homing fireball that flies at the player at full speed is seeking. When the player dodges, it shoots past and turns around.

B0403.heard: A red threat sits in the middle. Flea is the opposite of seek. The agent steers directly away from a target. Here it flees for 1.6 seconds until it is 300 pixels from the threat and then it stops steering. For example, a chicken in a farm level that runs from the player whenever the player comes near and settles once it is far enough away is fleeing.

B0404.heard: Arrive means seek, then slow down to stop at the target. Inside the last 200 pixels, the desired speed falls, so the agent eases in. After 6.9 seconds, it is about 6 pixels from the target and moving at under 5 pixels per second. Seek never slows and arrive does. For example, a pet that runs to the player and comes to a gentle stop at the player's feet instead of bumping past is arriving.

B0501.heard: Two chasers, gray and red, go after a black target that runs of steady 63 pixels per second in a simulated run, pursuing steer toward where a moving target will be not where it is now. The red chaser pursues and catches it at 2.6 seconds. The gray one seeks and catches it at 3 seconds, both move at 110. For example, a hawk enemy that dives at the spot a running player is about to reach is pursuing.

B0502.heard: One agent wandering, wander means small random turns, so the path meanders. Each ticket nudges a target point, the red dot around a small circle 100 pixels ahead and steers toward it. The turns are random but seeded, so a test can replay the same path. For example, a slime that drifts around a cave when it has nothing to chase, and drifts the same way in every test run, is wandering with a seed.

B0601.heard: Fourteen small agents in one room in a simulated run. Separation means steer away from near neighbors. Each agent turns away from any neighbor nearer than 60 pixels, the red ring. The nearest pair opens from 24 pixels apart to 43. For example, a crowd of zombies shuffling toward the player keeps a little space between each one, so they never pile up into a single blob.

B0602.heard: Alignment means steer to match the neighbors heading. Each agent turns toward the average direction of the agents around it. Heading agreement rises from 0.17 to 1, which means every agent points the same way. For example, a flock of birds in the background of a level, where all of them bank together as soon as their neighbors turn, is using alignment.

B0603.heard: Cohesion means steer toward the neighbor's center. Each agent heads for the middle of the agents within 170 pixels, the red ring, the bunch, and the mean distance to the center falls from 99 pixels to 19. Separation pushes agents apart and cohesion pulls them together. For example, a pack of wolves that drifts back into one group after the player splits it up is showing cohesion.

B0604.heard: All three rules at once. Emergent behavior is complex group behavior that comes out of simple rules. No agent knows there's a flock yet one forms. Agreement is 0.94 and no two agents are nearer than 31 pixels. For example, nobody writes a herd script for the deer in a forest level. Each deer follows separation, alignment, and cohesion, and the herd emerges on its own.

B0701.heard: Five-lettered circles joined by lines. A graph is a set of points called nodes joined by edges, and each edge has a weight, its cost. The cheapest route starts at node A, then goes through C, B and D to F for total cost of 10. These weights are made up. For example, the rooms of a dungeon can be the nodes, the doors between them the edges, and a long corridor gets a higher weight.

B0702.heard: A room eight cells wide and six tall with walls and mud. A grid marks each cell solid or free and every free cell becomes a node. This room gives 38 nodes and 49 edges. Godose Stargrid 2D works this way, the light tool for grid games. For example, a tile puzzle game where enemies step from tile to tile can run a Stargrid 2D on its tile map layer.

B0703.heard: A navigation mesh marks where agents can walk with polygons instead of cells. Here the walkable cells merge into 10 polygons, so the same room needs 10 nodes instead of 38. Godot bakes the mesh once ahead of time. The grid has a node for every cell, and a navigation mesh has one for every polygon. For example, the Walker-Gard arena has a navigation region whose polygon covers the floor, leaves out the obstacle. And keeps a margin for the guard's size.

B0704.heard: A waypoint is a single point along a path usually placed by hand. Here 11 points cover the room with 13 edges, each one only where the straight line between two points is clear. The placement is made up. The bars compare the three maps, 38 cells, 10 polygons, 11 points. For example, the Walker Guard's patrol state walks it around a loop of waypoints set around the arena.

B0801.heard: The same room search from start to goal. Bread First Search expands outward one step at a time, like a ripple and ignores cost. It stops at the goal with a fewest steps 11, but its route crosses mud, so it costs 18. It expanded 36 cells. For example, on a board game map where every square costs the same, Bread First Search is enough to count how many moves a piece needs.

B0802.heard: Dykstra's pathfinding that always expands the open cell with the lowest cost so far, with no estimate of what is left. It counts each mud cell at 8, so it walks around the mud. Its route is 15 steps and costs 15 cheaper than bread first search after 34 cells. For example, if Swamp Tile's slow units down in your strategy game, Dykstra sends a unit the long way round on dry land.

B0803.heard: The Dykstra search froze in half way. The open and closed set are the two lists the search keeps. Open hold cells found but not yet expanded the red outlines. Closed hold cells already expanded the pink ones. Here five are open and 17 closed. The search ends when the goal is taken from the open set. For example, when an enemy asks for a route, each tile next to it goes into the open set and once expanded moves to the closed set for good.

B0901.heard: The room search with A star, the number in each cell is its F. A star is pathfinding that takes the open cell with the lowest F first, where F is G plus H. Cells that point toward the goal score lower so it expands just 25 cells yet finds the cost 15 route. Dijkstra spreads in every direction and A star leans toward the goal. For example, an enemy in a large level plots a route to the player after searching far fewer tiles.

B0902.heard: One moment broken down, F, G, and H are the three numbers behind A star, G is the cost paid so far. H is the estimated cost still to go, here the Manhattan distance, F is the total G plus H. The cell taken next has G4 plus H7 so F is 11, the top of the open list. For example, a guard four tiles into its walk with seven tiles still to go to the player has an F of 11.

B0903.heard: Bars compare the three searches on the same room. Bread first search expanded 36 cells and paid 18. Dykstra expanded 34 and paid 15. A star expanded 25 and also paid 15. A star finds a route as cheap as Dykstra's with less work. For example, in a level where many enemies ask for paths at the same moment, that saved work keeps the game running smoothly.

B1001.heard: Two points on a grid labeled B and A. Manhattan distance counts moves along the grid's axis only across and up, never on a diagonal. Here it is 5 across plus 3 up, which is 8. On a grid that moves in four directions, it is the true cost when nothing is in the way. For example, a robot in a tile game that moves one tile up, down, left or right, needs exactly its Manhattan distance and moves on an empty floor.

B1002.heard: Euclidean distance is the straight line distance, the length the ruler would measure. Here the straight line is 5.83 against 8 along the grid. It is never more than the Manhattan distance, so it never overestimates, but on a four-direction grid it is the weaker guide. For example, a check that asks whether a noise is within a set number of pixels of a guard measures Euclidean distance.

B1003.heard: Two A Star runs on a room with a column of mud. An admissible heuristic is an estimate that never overestimates the true cost, and with one A Star returns the cheapest path. On the left the honest estimate pays 13 after 21 expansions. On the right the estimate is multiplied by 4. It finishes after 10, but hurries through the mud and pays 21. For example, an atile game with four direction moves that each cost at least one. Manhattan distance is admissible.

B1101.heard: An agent follows a path across the room to its goal. Navigation Agent 2D is the go-doh node that follows a path on the navigation mesh. You set its target position and the navigation server returns a path. Each physics frame your code asks it for the next path position and moves toward it. The agent never moves the body itself. For example, the walker guard is a character body with a navigation Agent 2D inside it. And the guard's own move and slide called does the moving.

B1102.heard: The gray dashes are the raw path, turning at every cell, 16 points and 15 cells long. Path smoothing cuts corners from a path wherever the straight line is clear and keeps a corner only where the line would hit a wall. The red path has 6 points and is 14.1 cells long, same route fewer corners. For example, a guard that zigzags cell by cell down a diagonal hallway walks one straight line once its path is smoothed.

B1103.heard: Two agents head straight at each other. Local avoidance is steering around nearby obstacles and agents reacting to whatever is near on each tick. A path in its smoothing ignore other agents. Without avoidance, the two pass 12 pixels apart, which means they overlap. With it, they pass 89 pixels apart. For example, two guards whose patrol routes cross in a narrow corridor side step each other instead of walking through one another.

B1201.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. Site range tests only the distance, so the dot behind the bar counts as seen. Line of sight also tests that nothing blocks the line, so the same dot is not seen.

B1202.heard: Seek aims at the target and never slows so it swings past and comes back. Arrive aims at the same target, then slows down and settles on it.

B1203.heard: Dykstra expands in every direction by cost 34 cells here. A star adds H, the estimate to the goal, and leans toward it. 25 cells. Both pay 15.

B1204.heard: Separation steers away from near neighbors and hear the nearest pair ends 108 pixels apart. Cohesion steers toward the neighbor's center and the mean distance to it shrinks to 26 pixels. One spreads the other gathers.

B1301.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it beside a chart of what it does. Make the guard see the player becomes seen only within 340 pixels inside a 70 degree cone on a line that hits no wall. Six dots, then six, then three.

B1302.heard: Make it move smoothly to the door becomes arrive, slowing down inside 200 pixels of the target, with a max speed of 160. At 100 pixels away the speed is 80 and at 20 it is 16.

B1303.heard: Find the shortest way becomes a star on the grid with a Manhattan heuristic, stopping when the goal leaves the open set. Dykstra expands 34 cells and a star 25 for the same cost of 15.

B1304.heard: Make the crowd look natural becomes separation, alignment and cohesion on every agent with a fixed random seed. Without separation the nearest pair touches at zero pixels. With it they stay 31 pixels apart.

B1305.heard: Make its search after the player hides becomes, store the last known position, walk there, wait one second, then return to patrol. The guard walks 357 pixels at 120 pixels per second, three seconds, then searches for one.

B1401.heard: This is a checklist to run before you trust a game AI behavior. First, can the agent really see the target? Check all three tests, the range, the cone, and a clear line.

B1402.heard: Second is the steering right for the job. Seek, arrive, pursue, or flee. Each one moves differently and only one fits.

B1403.heard: Third, does the agent slow down and stop where it should, or does it seek straight past its target and circle back?

B1404.heard: Fourth is the map of grid, a navigation mesh, or a set of waypoints. And can you say why that one suits this level?

B1405.heard: Fifth is the search A star with a heuristic that never overestimates. An admissible estimate is what makes A star return the cheapest path.

B1406.heard: Sixth is every random choice seated so a test can replay it. Then say it exactly. Not make it smart but within 340 pixels, a 70 degree cone, seed 5.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap an agent's senses, decides and acts once on every tick. Site range is a distance only and line of sight needs a clear line. Seek never slows and arrive slows down to stop on the target. Separation, alignment and cohesion together make a flock emerge. Dykstra expands by cost so far and a star adds an estimate toward the goal. An admissible heuristic never overestimates so a star finds the cheapest path.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game AI terms with short game making cases one at a time. Use the term site range, line of sight, field of view cone, seek, arrive, pursue, separation, cohesion, dixtra, and A star. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms, game AI perception and pathfinding at Nick Bear Brown.
